parts: Lesson 7: Indian Languages and Literature-II — Summary

Old Apabhramsha took new forms. The alphabets of Ashoka's Brahmi were uneven; by Harsha's time the letters were regular. All scripts of present northern Indian languages except Urdu originated in old Brahmi (compare Gujarati, Hindi and Punjabi). Over 200 languages or dialects are spoken in India; twenty-two are in the Constitution (originally 15: Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kashmiri, Marathi, Oriya, Punjabi, Sanskrit, Sindhi, Urdu, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam; Nepali, Manipuri and Konkani were added later). Forms of Hindi: Braj Bhasha (Surdas, Bihari), Avadhi (Tulsidas), Bhojpuri, Magadhi, Maithili (Vidyapati), Rajasthani and Khadi Boli; Khusrau used Khadi Boli in the 13th century but its extensive literary use began in the 19th century.

Arabic and Persian came with the Turks and Mongols; Persian remained the court language for centuries. Urdu was born from the interaction of Turkish settlers and soldiers (after the conquest of Delhi in 1192) with the common people, a dialect that became a formal language in the Persian script, boosted in Bahmani states (Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bijapur, Berar), where it was called Dakshini. The earliest Urdu poet is Amir Khusrau (1253–1325), follower of Nizamuddin Auliya, with works such as Laila Majnun and Ayina-i-Sikandari; others: Ghalib, Zauq, Iqbal (Bang-i-Dara; 'Saare Jahan Se Achha'); prose: Ratan Nath Sarshar (Fasana-i-Azad), Premchand began in Urdu. The nazm is an Urdu form; Nawabs of Lucknow patronised it; the last Mughal Bahadur Shah Zafar wrote poetry; Pakistan has Urdu as state language. Persian literature: Babur's Tuzuk-i-Baburi (in Turkish, translated into Persian under Akbar), Humayun Nama, Akbar Nama and Ain-i-Akbari of Abul Fazl, Faizi, Badayuni, Chandra Bhan (Shah Jahan's days), Abdul Hamid Lahori's Badshah Nama, Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, Tabaqat-i-Alamgiri; Noorjahan was a Persian poetess; Akbar had the Mahabharata, Gita and Upanishads translated into Persian; Minhaj-us-Siraj, Zia Barani and Ibn Battuta wrote in Persian; Amir Khusrau and Amir Hasan Dehlvi wrote Persian poetry.

Regional languages grew with the Bhakti movement and Sanskrit declined; Prithviraj Raso (about Prithviraj Chauhan) is considered the first Hindi book; Hindi evolved between the 7th–8th and 14th centuries (Veergatha Kala, Adi Kala, patronised by Rajputs). Devotional poetry followed: Tulsidas's Ramcharit Manas (Avadhi) based on Valmiki's Ramayana but deifies Rama (Valmiki's is a human hero) and adds folk scenes; Surdas's Sur Sagar (Braj) shows Krishna as an infant, a prankster and a young man with the gopis; Mirabai (Rajasthani), Raskhan, Nandadas, Rahim, Bhushan, Bihari (Satsai), Kabir (formless God). Rabindranath Tagore won the 1913 Nobel Prize for Geetanjali. Hindi prose came into its own in the 19th century: Bharatendu Harishchandra, Mahavir Prasad Dwivedi, Bankim Chandra's novels in translation (Vande Mataram is from Anandamath), Swami Dayanand (Satyartha Prakash; advocated Hindi as the common language), Premchand (Urdu to Hindi), Nirala, Mahadevi Verma (first woman writer to highlight women's issues), Maithili Sharan Gupt, Jaishankar Prasad, Ramchandra Shukla, Shyam Sundar Das, Pant, Dinkar, Bachchan. These writers wrote with a purpose.

Bengali: Baptist Mission Press at Serampore (1800), Fort William College (1800); Chaitanya's hymns and Mangal Kavyas; William Carey wrote a Bengali grammar and an English–Bengali dictionary; Macaulay's victory (1835), Wood's Despatch (1854), universities of Calcutta, Madras and Bombay (1857); Ram Mohan Roy, Vidyasagar, Akshay Kumar Dutta, Bankim Chandra, Sharat Chandra, R.C. Dutt, Rabindranath Tagore; nationalist poetry of Qazi Nazrul Islam (Bengali) and Subramania Bharati (Tamil). Assamese: buranjis, Shankardeva (Vaishnavism), Lakshminath Bezbaruah. Oriya: Saraladasa, Upendra Bhanja, Fakirmohan Senapati. Punjabi: Gurmukhi and Persian scripts; Guru Nanak first poet; Sufi Farid; Guru Tegh Bahadur and Guru Gobind Singh; love stories of Heer–Ranjha, Sassi–Punnu, Sohni–Mahiwal; Waris Shah's Heer; Bulleh Shah's kafis; Bhai Vir Singh (Rana Surat Singh). Rajasthani: bards; Colonel Todd's Annals and Antiquities of Rajasthan; Mirabai. Gujarati: Narsi Mehta, Narmad, Govardhanram's Saraswatichandra, K.M. Munshi (Prithvi Vallabh). Sindhi: Sufis; Mirza Kalich Beg, Dewan Kauramal. Marathi: Jnaneshwar (13th century; kirtan tradition), Namdev, Eknath, Tukaram (greatest Bhakti poet), Ramdas (Shivaji's guru), Tilak's Kesari. Kashmiri: Kalhana's Rajatarangini (Sanskrit); Lal Ded (14th century, first to sing in Kashmiri), Habba Khatoon, Mahjoor, Nund Rishi, Dina Nath Nadim; literature lagged due to poverty, backwardness, lack of schools and Dogra preference for Dogri.

Europeans added new words to Indian languages. Missionaries published dictionaries and grammars, introduced lithographic presses for local-language literature and opened schools and colleges that taught local languages, producing an educated reading class. Indians wrote in English after 1835: Michael Madhusudan Dutt, Toru Dutt, Sarojini Naidu and Tagore (poetry); Surendranath Banerjea, Pherozeshah Mehta and Nehru (prose).
